content: The second is a unit of time and serves as the base unit of time in the International System of Units (SI). Subdivisions of the second, such as the millisecond (one-thousandth of a second) and the nanosecond (one-billionth of a second), are commonly used. While SI prefixes can theoretically be applied to create multiples of the second (e.g., kilosecond, equivalent to one thousand seconds), such units are rarely used in practice. Instead, non-SI units like the minute, hour, and day are more commonly employed, with their values increasing by multiples of 60 and 24, rather than by powers of ten as in the SI system. Under the International System of Units, the second is currently defined based on the properties of the cesium atom. Specifically, it is defined as the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the cesium-133 atom. This definition assumes the cesium atom is at rest and at a temperature of absolute zero (0 K). The ground state is further defined in the absence of any external magnetic field. This modern definition aligns with the ephemeris second, which was historically based on astronomical measurements. The internationally recognized symbol for the second is s, as specified in ISO 31-1. The realization of the standard second is described in detail in publications such as NIST Special Publication 330 and by the National Research Council of Canada. One international second is equivalent to: 1/60 of a minute, 1/3,600 of an hour, 1/86,400 of a day (as per the International Astronomical Union system of units), 1/31,557,600 of a Julian year (as per the International Astronomical Union system of units). Historically, the concept of dividing time into smaller units dates back to ancient civilizations. The Egyptians, as early as 2000 BCE, divided both daytime and nighttime into twelve hours each, resulting in hours of varying lengths depending on the season. Hellenistic astronomers like Hipparchus (circa 150 BCE) and Ptolemy (circa 150 CE) introduced the sexagesimal division of the day and used a mean hour (1/24 of a day). However, they did not use distinct names for smaller time units, instead relying on simple fractions of an hour. The Babylonians, after 300 BCE, used sexagesimal fractions to specify time to at least six decimal places, although they did not further subdivide smaller units of time sexagesimally. For example, they used six fractional sexagesimal places to describe the length of a year, even though they lacked the means to measure such small fractions of a day in real time. Similarly, they specified the mean synodic month as 29;31,50,8,20 days (four fractional sexagesimal positions), a value later repeated by Hipparchus and Ptolemy and still used in the Hebrew calendar, albeit restated as 29 days, 12 hours, and 793 halakim (where 1 hour = 1,080 halakim). In medieval times, the Muslim scholar Al-Biruni (circa 1000 CE) recorded the times of new moons in terms of days, hours, minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths after noon on Sundays. Similarly, in 1267, Roger Bacon, a medieval scientist, described the times of full moons using hours, minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths (horae, minuta, secunda, tertia, and quarta) after noon on specific calendar dates. While the term third for 1/60 of a second persists in some languages, such as Polish (tercja) and Arabic (ثالثة), the modern second is subdivided decimally. The second became measurable with the invention of pendulum clocks, which kept mean time (as opposed to the apparent time displayed by sundials). In 1670, William Clement added a seconds pendulum to Christian Huygens' original pendulum clock. The seconds pendulum, with a period of two seconds (one second for a forward swing and one second for a backward swing), enabled longcase clocks to tick seconds. From this point, a second hand rotating once per minute in a small subdial began to appear on precision clock faces. In 1956, the second was redefined in terms of the Earth's orbital motion around the Sun for a specific epoch, as it had become evident that the Earth's rotation on its axis was not sufficiently uniform to serve as a standard of time. The Earth's motion was described in Newcomb's Tables of the Sun, which provided a formula for the Sun's motion at the epoch 1900 based on astronomical observations made between 1750 and 1892. This definition was ratified by the Eleventh General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1960. The tropical year in this definition was not directly measured but calculated from a formula describing a mean tropical year that decreased linearly over time, hence the reference to a specific instantaneous tropical year. With the advent of atomic clocks, it was decided to base the definition of the second on atomic transitions rather than the Earth's motion. After years of research, Louis Essen (National Physical Laboratory, England) and William Markowitz (United States Naval Observatory) determined the relationship between the cesium atom's hyperfine transition frequency and the ephemeris second. Using a common-view measurement method based on signals from radio station WWV, they measured the Moon's orbital motion around the Earth and inferred the Sun's apparent motion in terms of time as measured by an atomic clock. As a result, in 1967, the Thirteenth General Conference on Weights and Measures redefined the second in the International System of Units as the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the cesium-133 atom's ground state. During the 1970s, it was recognized that gravitational time dilation caused variations in the second produced by atomic clocks depending on their altitude. A uniform second was achieved by correcting the output of each atomic clock to mean sea level (the rotating geoid), effectively lengthening the second slightly. This correction was applied in 1977 and formalized in 1980. In relativistic terms, the SI second is defined as the proper time on the rotating geoid. The definition was further refined in 1997 by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) to account for the effects of ambient temperature (black-body radiation) on atomic clocks and to extrapolate the value of the second accordingly. In recent decades, advancements in technology have enabled the confinement of ions to regions of space smaller than one cubic micron (10^-6 m^3). These ions are nearly completely isolated from their surroundings, suggesting the potential for frequency or time standards with reproducibility and stability several orders of magnitude superior to the best cesium time standards. Such standards are currently under development, including magneto-optical traps and trapped ion optical frequency standards.
